etymology: Welsh surname Bayly, a variant of bailiff, from Old French baillif, an officer or steward; the given name Lewis from the Frankish Chlodovech, “famous warrior.”
biblical_def: Lewis Bayly, chaplain to the household of King James and afterward Bishop of Bangor, is remembered less for any ecclesiastical dignity than for the little book that made him a household name in ten thousand godly homes: The Practice of Piety, Directing a Christian how to Walk that he may Please God. First printed in the early seventeenth century, it ran through edition upon edition, was carried across the sea to New England, and was one of the two books that Bunyan’s wife brought to their marriage — the very volumes, he tells us, that first stirred his conscience toward the things of God. Bayly wrote as a physician of souls, pressing upon the reader the meditation of God’s attributes, the misery of the man out of Christ, the blessedness of the man in Him, and the daily discipline of secret prayer, family worship, Sabbath-keeping, and holy dying. He would have every hour of the day sanctified, every meal begun and ended with thanksgiving, every night closed with self-examination. His genius was not novelty but application: he took the settled truths of the gospel and drove them home to the heart and the household. In an age of learned controversy he wrote for the ploughman and the goodwife, and by that plain, warm, methodical piety he did more to shape the devotional life of the English-speaking church than many a folio of divinity.
webster_summary: Jacobean bishop and author of The Practice of Piety, the most widely read English devotional manual of its age.
webster_full: Lewis Bayly (d. 1631), Welsh-born divine, chaplain to King James I and Bishop of Bangor.
Author of The Practice of Piety, a methodical guide to personal, family, and Sabbath devotion.
His book passed through scores of editions and was translated into many tongues across Europe.
One of two volumes brought by John Bunyan’s first wife, instrumental in awakening his early conscience.
A representative of the warm, practical divinity that marked the Elizabethan and Jacobean Puritans.
scriptures: But refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of practical, daily piety.
corruption_paragraphs: Bayly’s name is preserved not because any modern party has troubled to revise it, but because the age has largely forgotten the very thing he taught: that godliness is a practice, a daily discipline of the heart before God, and not a mood or an occasional sentiment. Where his book once sat beside the Bible on the shelf of the poorest cottage, the modern professor of religion often keeps no method of devotion at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the practice of piety itself — that walk with God which Bayly directed step by step, from the morning meditation to the evening self-examination. Sound doctrine is meant to be lived; the truths of the gospel are given not merely to be believed in the head but to be exercised in the closet, the family, and the Sabbath assembly, until the whole of life is brought under the eye of God.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed conviction that saving faith bears fruit in ordered, daily godliness.
roots_lines: The Puritan doctrine of sanctification as a lifelong, methodical walk with God.
Family religion — household worship as the seedbed of the church and commonwealth.
Sabbath-keeping as a delight and a discipline appointed for the soul’s rest in God.
Secret prayer and self-examination as the daily armour of the Christian life.
The plain, applicatory preaching and writing of the practical English divines.
usage: Bayly’s Practice of Piety shaped the devotional habits of generations of English-speaking believers.
A pastor may commend Bayly’s method as a pattern for ordering the Christian’s day around God.
The book’s influence on Bunyan links the practical divines to the greatest of the Puritan allegorists.

etymology: English surname Dod, of Old English origin, perhaps from a personal name or a rounded, thickset form; the given name John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Dod, so beloved for his labours upon the Ten Commandments that he was known throughout the land as “Decalogue Dod,” was one of the most venerable of the Jacobean Puritan preachers, a man whose long life reached from the days of Elizabeth into the very heat of the civil troubles. With his fellow-labourer Robert Cleaver he set forth A Plaine and Familiar Exposition of the Ten Commandements, a work that taught a generation to read the moral law not as a dead letter but as the abiding rule of a holy life, spiritual in its reach, searching the very thoughts and affections of the heart. Silenced more than once for his nonconformity, he bore deprivation without bitterness and preached wherever a door was opened to him, drawing the affections of the common people by a homely, proverbial wisdom that made him a treasury of godly sayings long remembered in the mouths of plain Christians. His counsel was sought by the great and the lowly alike; his patience under suffering preached as loudly as his sermons. In an age tempted to loosen the law once grace was preached, Dod held forth the perfect harmony of the two, showing that the same gospel which frees a man from the curse of the law establishes the law as the delight of his renewed heart.
webster_summary: Long-lived Puritan preacher called “Decalogue Dod” for his celebrated exposition of the Ten Commandments.
webster_full: John Dod (c. 1549–1645), Puritan minister of Elizabethan and Jacobean England.
Co-author with Robert Cleaver of a widely used plain exposition of the Ten Commandments.
Nicknamed “Decalogue Dod” for his mastery of the moral law and its application.
Repeatedly silenced for nonconformity, yet reverenced for patience and homely godly wisdom.
A fountain of proverbial sayings long treasured among plain English Christians.
scriptures: Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
Rom 7:12
Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.
Mat 5:17
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the abiding, spiritual use of God’s law.
corruption_paragraphs: Dod’s name has drawn no revisionist assault, for the modern mind has simply let the moral law slip from memory. Where he taught the Ten Commandments as a searching rule for every thought and affection, the present age often treats the law either as an abolished relic or as a set of outward rules easily kept; the spiritual, heart-searching depth that Dod pressed home is what has been lost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the third use of the law — that same law, written now upon the heart of the regenerate, becomes the believer’s delight and the pattern of his gratitude. Dod’s life recovers the truth that grace does not abolish the commandment but establishes it, and that the man who loves the Saviour will love the law which images His holiness.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of the moral law as the perpetual, spiritual rule of the Christian life.
roots_lines: The abiding authority of the moral law summarized in the Ten Commandments.
The spiritual interpretation of the law reaching to the thoughts and affections of the heart.
The harmony of law and gospel — grace freeing from the curse, the law remaining the rule.
Patient endurance of silencing and deprivation for conscience’ sake.
Plain, proverbial, affectionate preaching that reaches the common people.
usage: “Decalogue Dod” became a byword for the Puritan mastery of the moral law.
Dod’s exposition taught congregations to search their hearts by every commandment.
His patient bearing of silencing is cited as a model of nonconformist meekness.

etymology: English surname Bolton, from Old English bothl-tun, “a settlement with a dwelling”; the given name Robert from Germanic Hrodebert, “bright in fame.”
biblical_def: Robert Bolton, minister at Broughton in Northamptonshire, was a preacher of uncommon power whose ministry was itself a monument of grace, for in his younger days he had been a scoffer and a stranger to true religion, until the LORD arrested him with such a mighty and terrifying conviction of sin that he was, in his own account, cast down as one dead before he was raised up in the comforts of the gospel. Out of that experience came a ministry that could break the hard heart and bind up the broken, for he knew both the terrors of the law and the consolations of Christ from the inside. His Some General Directions for a Comfortable Walking with God is a masterwork of practical divinity, tracing the whole course of the believer from his first awakening through the daily walk of communion with God to the hour of death; and his Instructions for a Right Comforting Afflicted Consciences stands among the tenderest of the Puritan casuistical treatises, a physic for the wounded spirit. Bolton preached with such gravity and searching application that men trembled under his word, yet he was equally skilled to pour the oil and wine of the gospel into the conscience wounded by sin. He died in the assurance he had preached, bidding his hearers remember what he had taught them.
webster_summary: Powerful Jacobean Puritan preacher, converted from profligacy, author of directions for a comfortable walking with God.
webster_full: Robert Bolton (1572–1631), Puritan minister at Broughton, Northamptonshire.
Converted out of a scoffing, ungodly youth by a deep and terrifying work of conviction.
Author of Some General Directions for a Comfortable Walking with God.
Wrote a tender treatise on rightly comforting afflicted consciences.
Preached with searching power that could both break and heal the heart.
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Gen 5:24
And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.
Isa 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the reality of thorough conviction and comfortable communion.
corruption_paragraphs: No modern school has cared to redefine Bolton, yet the very substance of his ministry has fallen out of favour. He preached a deep, humbling conviction of sin as the ordinary way into gospel comfort; the present age, impatient of any wound, wants the balm without the lancet, and so knows little of the settled, well-grounded peace that Bolton laboured to build upon the ruins of self-righteousness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the biblical order of the gospel: the law humbling the sinner before grace comforts him, and a walk with God that is comfortable precisely because it is honest about sin. Bolton’s treatises recover the Puritan physic of souls — a searching, tender casuistry that neither flatters the presumptuous nor crushes the contrite, but leads the awakened conscience by sure steps into the peace of Christ.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed pattern of conviction, conversion, and communion with God through Christ.
roots_lines: The necessity of thorough conviction of sin as preparation for gospel comfort.
Sovereign, effectual grace arresting the scoffer and raising the dead heart.
Practical divinity directing the whole course of the believer’s walk with God.
The casuistry of comforting afflicted and wounded consciences.
Death in assurance as the seal of a faithful gospel ministry.
usage: Bolton’s conversion is cited as a striking instance of sovereign grace overtaking a scoffer.
His Comfortable Walking with God remains a classic of Puritan practical divinity.
Pastors draw on his casuistry when ministering to consciences wounded by sin.

etymology: English surname Rogers, “son of Roger,” from Germanic Hrodgar, “famous spear”; the given name Daniel from Hebrew Daniyyel, “God is my judge.”
biblical_def: Daniel Rogers, lecturer at Wethersfield in Essex, was a son of that remarkable godly stock which gave the English church a whole household of faithful preachers, being of the same family as Richard Rogers the author of the Seven Treatises and near kin to the martyr-line that reached back to John Rogers of Smithfield. A learned and painful divine, he laboured many years in that county which was a very nursery of Puritanism, and set forth weighty treatises of practical godliness, among them his large work on Matrimoniall Honour, wherein he unfolded the honour, duties, and holy ordering of marriage as a covenant instituted of God and a picture of Christ and His church. He was a man of fervent, searching spirit, known for the heat and earnestness of his preaching, and though at times troubled for his nonconformity he continued to feed the flock committed to him. Rogers stood in that Essex company of divines — the Rogerses, the Roberts, the lecturers of the eastern counties — who by their combined labours made that region a stronghold of experimental religion, so that many afterward crossed the sea to plant the same seed in New England. His life bears witness to the covenant faithfulness of God, who often blesses a godly family with generation upon generation of faithful ministers.
webster_summary: Learned Puritan lecturer of Wethersfield, Essex, of the godly Rogers stock, author on the honour of marriage.
webster_full: Daniel Rogers (1573–1652), Puritan minister and lecturer at Wethersfield in Essex.
Of the notable Rogers family that gave the English church many faithful preachers.
Author of Matrimoniall Honour, a large practical treatise on Christian marriage.
Laboured in Essex, a chief nursery of experimental Puritan religion.
Known for fervent, searching preaching despite trouble for nonconformity.
scriptures: Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Pro 22:1
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his labours recover the honour of marriage and household godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: Rogers has suffered no learned revision, yet the truth he most fully expounded has been overturned in our day more thoroughly than almost any other: the honour, permanence, and God-ordained order of marriage. Where he taught wedlock as a holy covenant imaging Christ and His church, the modern mind has severed marriage from its Author, emptied it of its complementary order, and made it a merely private and dissoluble arrangement.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of marriage as God appointed it — one man and one woman, joined in covenant for life, the husband loving as Christ loved, the wife honouring as the church honours her Lord. Rogers’ treatise recovers the truth that the Christian household is a school of godliness and a living picture of the gospel, to be reverenced and rightly ordered before God.
roots_summary: Rooted in the covenant faithfulness of God shown in godly families and the holy ordering of marriage.
roots_lines: The covenant blessing of God upon godly families and their generations.
Marriage as a divine institution imaging Christ and His church.
The complementary duties of husband and wife under the word of God.
Experimental, searching preaching in the Essex nursery of Puritanism.
Faithful labour in a lecture ministry despite the pressures of conformity.
usage: The Rogers family is cited as a signal instance of God’s covenant mercy to godly households.
Daniel Rogers’ Matrimoniall Honour is drawn upon in Reformed teaching on marriage.
Essex under such lecturers became a byword for experimental Puritan religion.

etymology: English surname Whately, from a place-name meaning “wheat clearing” (Old English hwāte + lēah); the given name William from Germanic Willahelm, “resolute protector.”
biblical_def: William Whately, vicar of Banbury in Oxfordshire, was so mighty and vehement in the pulpit that he was called “the roaring boy of Banbury,” a name that fastened upon him not for any disorder but for the thunder of his preaching and the earnest zeal with which he pressed the word upon the consciences of his hearers. Banbury under his ministry became a proverb for godliness — a “Banbury saint” was the scoffer’s term for one precise in religion — and the profane of that country felt the edge of his rebukes. Trained in the schools and thoroughly furnished in the tongues, he yet spent his strength in plain and powerful application, being one of that company of practical divines who sought not to display learning but to save souls. He wrote helpfully upon the Christian life and household duties, including his treatises on the ordering of marriage, and his sermons were marked by a fervent, arresting delivery that seized the attention of even the careless. Whately laboured his whole ministry in that one place, wearing himself out in preaching, catechizing, and the pastoral care of his flock, and left behind him a town so seasoned with the gospel that his memory long remained a savour of life to the godly and a reproof to the ungodly.
webster_summary: Fervent Jacobean preacher of Banbury, called “the roaring boy” for the thunder and zeal of his pulpit.
webster_full: William Whately (1583–1639), Puritan vicar of Banbury, Oxfordshire.
Nicknamed “the roaring boy of Banbury” for his powerful, vehement preaching.
Under his ministry Banbury became a proverb for precise godliness.
Learned in the tongues yet devoted to plain, searching application.
Wrote on the Christian life and the right ordering of marriage.
scriptures: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the power and zeal of plain gospel preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: Whately’s memory faces no revisionist campaign, yet the manner of ministry he embodied — fervent, plain, unsparing, aimed at the conscience — has grown strange in a temperate and man-pleasing age. Where he thundered the word like a hammer that breaks the rock, the modern pulpit often prefers a soothing and inoffensive address that leaves the sinner untroubled and the saint unstirred.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the power of preaching — not the roar of mere vehemence, but the demonstration of the Spirit that makes the plain word of God a fire and a hammer to the heart. Whately’s ministry recovers the truth that a town may be seasoned with the gospel through the faithful, zealous, unwearied preaching of one man who spends himself for the souls of his people.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed conviction that the preached word, attended by the Spirit, is the power of God to save.
roots_lines: Preaching as the ordained means by which God saves and sanctifies His people.
Fervent, plain, conscience-searching application over the display of learning.
The reforming effect of faithful preaching upon a whole town or region.
Pastoral perseverance — a lifetime spent in one flock’s care.
The scorn of the ungodly (“Banbury saint”) borne as a badge of gospel fidelity.
usage: “The roaring boy of Banbury” became a byword for zealous Puritan preaching.
Banbury under Whately illustrates a town reformed by one man’s faithful pulpit.
His sermons are cited as models of fervent, applicatory practical divinity.

etymology: English surname Capel, from Old French capele, “chapel”; the given name Richard from Germanic Ricohard, “strong ruler.”
biblical_def: Richard Capel, a learned and godly minister of Gloucestershire, is chiefly remembered for his searching treatise Tentations, their Nature, Danger, Cure, one of the most penetrating anatomies of temptation that the Puritan age produced. A scholar of Oxford who resigned his living rather than read the Book of Sports and profane the Sabbath, he retired to the practice of physic and to private study, yet continued to counsel troubled souls and to labour among the godly of his county. In his treatise he opened the whole secret war of temptation — how the flesh, the world, and the devil assault the soul, how sin gains entrance through the imagination and the affections, and by what means of watchfulness, mortification, prayer, and the word the Christian may be armed and healed. He wrote as a physician of both body and soul, tracing the disease to its root and prescribing the sovereign remedy that is in Christ. Capel understood, as few have written so plainly, that the believer’s life is a warfare, that indwelling sin must be daily crucified, and that the tempted saint is not thereby cast off but is being trained in humility and dependence. His work stands beside Owen’s later treatises as a guide for those who would understand and resist the deceitfulness of their own hearts.
webster_summary: Godly Gloucestershire minister, author of Tentations, a searching Puritan anatomy of temptation and its cure.
webster_full: Richard Capel (1586–1656), Oxford-trained Puritan minister of Gloucestershire.
Resigned his living rather than read the Book of Sports and profane the Sabbath.
Author of Tentations, their Nature, Danger, Cure, a classic on temptation.
Practised physic and continued to counsel troubled and afflicted consciences.
A forerunner, with Capel’s own generation, of Owen’s treatises on indwelling sin.
scriptures: Jam 1:14
But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his work recovers the doctrine of mortification and the warfare against sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Capel’s treatise has met no modern redefinition, but the doctrine it defends has been widely abandoned. Where he anatomized temptation as a deadly enemy to be watched, resisted, and slain, the present age tends to excuse the desire and rename the sin, treating the very stirrings of lust that Capel would have mortified as identity to be affirmed rather than corruption to be crucified.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the daily mortification of indwelling sin — the truth, as Capel and Owen alike pressed it, that the believer must be killing sin or it will be killing him. His Tentations recovers the sober knowledge of the heart’s deceitfulness, the reality of the spiritual warfare, and the sufficiency of Christ, by whom alone the tempted soul is armed, healed, and finally delivered.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of mortification and the believer’s warfare against indwelling sin.
roots_lines: The nature of temptation — how the flesh, world, and devil assault the soul.
The mortification of indwelling sin through the Spirit and the word.
Watchfulness and prayer as the appointed guard against entering temptation.
Sabbath-keeping and refusal to profane God’s day even at personal cost.
The sufficiency of Christ as the sovereign remedy for the tempted saint.
usage: Capel’s Tentations is prized as a searching Puritan guide to resisting temptation.
His refusal of the Book of Sports is cited as a stand for the Sabbath’s sanctity.
Reformed teachers pair his work with Owen’s on the mortification of sin.

etymology: English surname Taylor, from Old French tailleur, “a cutter of cloth”; the given name Thomas from Aramaic tē’ōmā, “twin.”
biblical_def: Thomas Taylor, a learned Cambridge divine of the Jacobean age, was among the most able of the Puritan expositors, remembered especially for his work upon the types and shadows of the Old Testament, wherein he traced with care how the ceremonies, persons, and appointments of the elder covenant pointed forward to Christ. His treatise Christ Revealed, or the Old Testament Explained gathered the types of Scripture and showed their fulfilment in the Lord Jesus, teaching the church to read Moses and the prophets as a veiled gospel and to find the Saviour in every shadow of the ceremonial law. So bold and early was he in the cause of reformation that he preached against the corruptions of Rome while yet a young man in the university, and he continued a faithful and painful preacher, latterly in London, expounding whole books of Scripture with solid learning and warm application. Taylor stood in that noble tradition of Reformed exposition which held that the Old Testament and the New are one covenant of grace under differing administrations, Christ being the substance of both. His labours upon the types furnished the church with a treasury for the preaching of Christ from all the Scriptures, and taught believers to see the unity of the word and the constancy of the gospel from the foundation of the world.
webster_summary: Learned Jacobean Puritan expositor, author of Christ Revealed, a study of the Old Testament types fulfilled in Christ.
webster_full: Thomas Taylor (1576–1632), Cambridge-trained Puritan divine and expositor.
Author of Christ Revealed, or the Old Testament Explained, on the types of Scripture.
Preached boldly against Roman corruptions while a young man at the university.
A painful expositor of whole books of Scripture, latterly ministering in London.
A representative of the Reformed reading of the Old Testament as a veiled gospel.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Heb 10:1

For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
Joh 5:39

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his work recovers the unity of the covenants and Christ in all Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Taylor’s exposition faces no modern party bent on revising it, yet the manner of reading Scripture he practised has been assailed at its foundation. Where he found Christ in the types and shadows of the Old Testament and held the two Testaments to be one covenant of grace, the historical-critical spirit of the last age has sought to sunder the Scriptures, to deny their unity, and to strip the Old Testament of its testimony to the Saviour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Christ-centred unity of the whole Bible — that from Moses and all the prophets the Lord expounded the things concerning Himself, and that the ceremonies of the law were a shadow whose body is Christ. Taylor’s labours recover the church’s ancient confidence that the same gospel runs from Genesis to Revelation, and that the tabernacle, the sacrifices, and the types all preach the coming and finished work of the Redeemer.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of the one covenant of grace and Christ as the substance of the Scriptures.
roots_lines: The typology of the Old Testament fulfilled in the person and work of Christ.
The unity of the covenants — one covenant of grace under differing administrations.
The reading of the ceremonial law as a veiled preaching of the gospel.
Bold, early opposition to the corruptions of Rome in the cause of reformation.
Painful, learned exposition of whole books of Scripture with warm application.
usage: Taylor’s Christ Revealed is a standard Puritan source on Old Testament typology.
His work teaches preachers to find Christ in the shadows of the ceremonial law.
He is cited for the Reformed unity of the Old and New Testaments in one gospel.

etymology: English surname Baynes, a variant of Baines, perhaps from Old English bān, “bone,” or a place-name; the given name Paul from Latin Paulus, “small, humble.”
biblical_def: Paul Baynes, who succeeded the great William Perkins in the lecture at Great St. Andrew’s in Cambridge, was a link of gold in that chain of godly Cambridge preachers by whom the light of experimental religion was passed from hand to hand: converted, it was said, under the ministry that Perkins had established, he in turn became the instrument of the conversion of Richard Sibbes, who begat John Cotton, who begat John Preston, so that a whole lineage of eminent divines traced its spiritual descent to Baynes. Silenced early for his nonconformity and reduced to great poverty, he bore his afflictions with a rare cheerfulness and continued to write and counsel, leaving behind him an Exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians that is among the richest of Puritan commentaries, unfolding with spiritual depth the doctrines of sovereign election, effectual calling, and the believer’s union with Christ and standing in heavenly places. His shorter Letters and treatises breathe the same tender, searching, heavenly spirit. Baynes was not a man of station or wealth, but of grace; poor in this world, he was rich in faith and made many rich by his ministry. His life is a bright testimony to the sovereignty of God, who chooses the weak and lowly to carry His gospel and to father, under Him, whole generations of faithful men.
webster_summary: Puritan successor to William Perkins at Cambridge, author of a rich exposition of Ephesians and spiritual father of Sibbes.
webster_full: Paul Baynes (d. 1617), Puritan preacher who succeeded William Perkins in his Cambridge lecture.
Instrument of the conversion of Richard Sibbes, beginning a famous chain of godly divines.
Author of a spiritually rich Exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians.
Silenced for nonconformity and reduced to poverty, which he bore with cheerful faith.
A witness to God’s use of the poor and lowly to father generations in the gospel.
scriptures: Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:6
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers sovereign election and the fruitful chain of godly ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: Baynes has drawn no revisionist attention, yet the doctrines his commentary most gloried in — sovereign election, effectual calling, union with Christ — are precisely those the man-centred spirit of the age most resents. Where Baynes traced the whole of salvation to God’s eternal choice before the foundation of the world, the modern religion of self would place the decisive power in the will of the creature.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of grace in salvation, together with the fruitfulness God appoints to faithful, hidden ministry. Baynes, poor and silenced, was made the spiritual father of Sibbes and, through him, of a whole lineage of divines; his life recovers the truth that God chooses the weak things of the world, and that the labours of an obscure and afflicted servant may bear a harvest of grace for generations.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrines of sovereign election, effectual calling, and union with Christ.
roots_lines: Sovereign, unconditional election unto salvation before the foundation of the world.
Effectual calling by which the Spirit draws the chosen to Christ.
The believer’s union with Christ and standing in heavenly places.
God’s use of the poor, weak, and afflicted to carry His gospel.
The fruitful chain of godly ministry passed from Perkins to Baynes to Sibbes.

etymology: English surname Rogers, “son of Roger,” from Germanic Hrodgar, “famous spear”; the given name Richard from Germanic Ricohard, “strong ruler.”
biblical_def: Richard Rogers, lecturer at Wethersfield in Essex, was one of the fathers of English practical divinity, whose Seven Treatises was reckoned the first great methodical handbook of the Christian life to appear from a Puritan pen, gathering into an orderly whole the doctrine and duties of experimental religion. Therein he traced the way of a soul from its estate by nature through effectual calling into the daily practice of godliness, unfolding the marks of a true believer, the ordering of the heart, the private and public means of grace, and the whole discipline of walking with God. He was famous also for the covenant into which he and certain of his brethren entered, binding themselves before God to a stricter watchfulness and holiness, and for the diary in which he recorded the frames of his soul, his conflicts with sin, and his renewed resolutions — a monument of the searching self-examination that marked the godly of his day. When a courtier once mocked him for taking so much pains in religion, Rogers is said to have answered that he served a precise God. Silenced at times for nonconformity, he laboured many years in that Essex nursery of Puritanism, and by his book, his covenant, and his example he did more than almost any of his generation to give shape and method to the pursuit of holiness.
webster_summary: Father of English practical divinity, author of the Seven Treatises, lecturer of Wethersfield in Essex.
webster_full: Richard Rogers (1551–1618), Puritan lecturer at Wethersfield in Essex.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers methodical, watchful, self-examining holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Rogers has met no learned revision, but the strict and watchful holiness he practised is now scorned by the very name once flung at him — precisianism. Where he walked circumspectly, kept a diary of his soul, and served a precise God, the modern spirit calls such earnestness legalism or morbid introspection, and prefers a religion that costs nothing and searches nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the diligent, methodical pursuit of holiness — the walking circumspectly, the examining of oneself whether we be in the faith, the ordered use of the means of grace that Rogers reduced to method in his Seven Treatises. His life recovers the truth that holiness is no accident but a discipline, and that the God who has called us is Himself holy and precise, and will be served with reverence and godly fear.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of practical, methodical sanctification and watchful self-examination.

etymology: English surname Preston, from Old English prēost-tūn, “priest’s settlement”; the given name John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Preston, master of Emmanuel College in Cambridge — that seminary of Puritanism — and one of the most influential preachers of his generation, was a man of rare gifts who might have risen to any height at court, yet gave himself wholly to the cause of the gospel and the training of a godly ministry. Converted under the preaching of John Cotton, and standing in that golden chain of Cambridge divines that reached back through Sibbes and Baynes to Perkins, he became a physician of souls whose sermons drew multitudes and whose influence reached even into the councils of state. His posthumous works — among them The Breastplate of Faith and Love, The New Covenant, and The Saints Qualification — are treasuries of covenant divinity and experimental religion, unfolding the freeness of grace, the nature of saving faith, and the everlasting covenant that God makes with His people in Christ. He preached faith and love as the very breastplate by which the Christian is guarded, tracing the marks of the one and the fruits of the other. Cut off in the midst of his usefulness, dying while still a young man, he committed his soul to the covenant God he had preached, and left the church a body of writing by which he, being dead, yet speaketh, teaching the assurance of faith and the sweetness of union with Christ.
webster_summary: Influential master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and covenant divine, author of The Breastplate of Faith and Love.
webster_full: John Preston (1587–1628), master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and eminent Puritan preacher.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his works recover covenant grace and the assurance of saving faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Preston’s memory faces no revisionist campaign, yet the covenant divinity he preached — the free grace of God pledged in an everlasting covenant, laid hold of by a faith that works by love — is little understood in an age that has largely lost the very grammar of covenant. Where Preston set forth God binding Himself by promise to be a God to His people, the modern spirit conceives of religion as a private and contractless sentiment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant of grace and the assurance it affords — that God has established an everlasting covenant in Christ, that saving faith rests upon His pledged word, and that the believer may put on faith and love as a breastplate against every assault. Preston’s works recover the sweetness of gospel assurance grounded not in the changeable self but in the unchanging promise of the covenant-keeping God.
roots_summary: Rooted in the Reformed doctrine of the covenant of grace and the assurance of saving faith.
roots_lines: The everlasting covenant of grace by which God pledges Himself to His people in Christ.

Assurance grounded in God’s unchanging promise, not the believer’s frames.
